**Rotational analogue of force**
Torque is the rotational counterpart of force: just as a net force causes linear acceleration, a net torque causes angular acceleration. It is symbolized by the Greek letter tau and is the standard giveaway for this answer.

**Cross product of position (lever arm) and force**
Torque is defined as tau = r × F, where r is the vector from the rotation axis to the point where the force is applied. Its magnitude is rF sin θ, so a force pointing along the lever arm produces zero torque, and the right-hand rule gives its direction (the thumb points along the torque vector).

**Time derivative of angular momentum**
Net external torque equals dL/dt, the rate of change of angular momentum. When there is no net external torque, angular momentum is conserved.

**Moment of inertia times angular acceleration (I times alpha)**
The rotational form of Newton's second law states that net torque equals I·α, where I is the moment of inertia and α is the angular acceleration. "Moment of inertia" itself is not an acceptable answer.

**Gyroscopic (torque-induced) precession**
When a torque acts perpendicular to a spinning object's angular momentum, the spin axis slowly rotates instead of falling over. Examples include a gyroscope, a spinning top, and a bicycle wheel hung from one end of its axle. Precession is described as either "torque-induced" or "torque-free," and a top's precession rate equals torque divided by its angular momentum. Induced precession changes the first Euler angle.

**Torque on a current loop or magnetic dipole (tau = μ × B = NIAB sin θ)**
A current-carrying loop in a magnetic field feels a torque equal to the cross product of its magnetic moment and the field. For a loop of N turns this is NIAB sin θ, and it is greatest when the field lies in the plane of the loop. This is how electric motors and galvanometers work.

**Torque on an electric dipole (tau = p × E)**
In a uniform electric field, a dipole with moment p feels a torque p × E (magnitude qEd sin θ). This torque turns the dipole until it lines up with the field, where the net torque is zero.

**Work as the integral of torque over angle; power as torque times angular velocity**
The work done by a torque is the integral of tau dθ. Power is the dot product of torque and angular velocity (P = τ·ω), so torque also equals power divided by angular velocity (P/2πν, where ν is the rotation frequency).

**Newton-meter (units with the same dimensions as energy)**
The SI unit of torque is the newton-meter; foot-pounds are also used. It has the same dimensions as the joule, but it is not energy and is often written as joules per radian. Torque wrenches measure it so mechanics do not over-tighten bolts, and "cheater bars" lengthen a wrench to increase it.

**Euler's equations and Poinsot's ellipsoid**
Euler's equations for rigid-body rotation relate the torque components (sometimes written M) to the principal moments of inertia, the angular velocity, and the angular acceleration. Poinsot's construction, in which the inertia ellipsoid rolls on a fixed plane, shows how a rigid body moves when the torque is zero, as in an Euler top.

**Varignon's theorem**
This theorem from statics, named for Pierre Varignon, states that the moment (torque) of a resultant force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its component forces. In other words, torques from concurrent forces add.

**Trouton-Noble experiment**
This 1903 experiment looked for a torque on a charged capacitor that should appear if the capacitor moved through a stationary ether. No such torque was found, and this null result supports special relativity.

**Gear trains and torque multipliers (planetary/epicyclic gears)**
When an output gear has more teeth than its input gear, the gear train reduces speed and increases torque. Gearboxes that do this, including epicyclic gearsets made of "sun" and "planet" gears, are called torque multipliers.

**Breakdown, pull-in, and cogging torque in motors**
In an induction motor, the breakdown torque is the maximum torque, found where the derivative of torque with respect to slip is zero. Stepper motors have pull-in torque values, and cogging torque comes from attraction between the rotor magnets and the stator, which makes motion jerky at low speeds.

**Rotational equilibrium (levers, pulleys, and couples)**
An object does not start rotating when the net torque on it is zero, as with a balanced lever. For a pulley, the torque from the rope is the tension times the disk's radius. A couple, a pair of equal and opposite forces that act along different lines, produces a nonzero torque even though the net force is zero.
